Fertilised ova of the purple sea urchin Strongylocentrotus purpuratus are approximately 80 micrometres in diameter, and the resulting zygotes develop into free-swimming blastulae within hours of gamete fusion. At a sustained water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], the time required from fertilisation through the bipinnaria and pluteus larval stages to the attainment of metamorphic competence is approximately 45 days after birth . This duration reflects the relatively slow developmental rates typical of temperate echinoids reared under cooler conditions. Once the pluteus larva possesses a fully formed adult rudiment, it settles onto a suitable substratum and undergoes metamorphic climax, a process involving rapid arm resorption and the reorganisation of the bilaterally symmetrical larval body plan into the radially symmetrical juvenile form. The recently metamorphosed juvenile then commences benthic grazing, transitioning from endogenous yolk reserves to exogenous feeding on biofilm diatoms and coralline algae.

The test diameter at which the majority of individuals first become reproductively active, marking the onset of puberty, has been measured at 2.5 centimetres [Lp = 2.5 centimetres]. Field surveys of wild populations in the kelp forests of southern California indicate that the smallest adults observed participating in spawning aggregations typically possess a test diameter near this size. Published records note that the diameter at first spawning is approximately 4 centimetres, indicating a lag between the initial attainment of gametogenic capability and the first successful broadcast fertilisation event. The body mass of an individual that has just reached this pubertal size is approximately 7.3 grams [Wwp = approximately 7.3 grams] wet weight, a figure derived from the length-weight relationship established for the congener Strongylocentrotus droebachiensis. This value is consistent with the modest energetic investment required for a juvenile to allocate resources toward gonadal development while still prioritising further somatic growth of the test and lantern apparatus.

The maximum test diameter ever recorded for Strongylocentrotus purpuratus in natural settings is 10 centimetres [Li = 10 centimetres], a size that corresponds to the asymptotic limit achieved by the oldest and largest individuals within a given cohort. At this ultimate test diameter, the estimated whole-body wet weight is 465 grams [Wwi = 465 grams], based on scaling relationships derived from morphometric data in related species. The purple sea urchin does not exhibit indeterminate growth; instead, growth rates decelerate markedly after sexual maturation, with the annual increment in test diameter becoming very small in the largest size classes. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) has been reported at approximately 21% [GSI = approximately 21%] for animals maintained experimentally at a temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This value is within the range observed for temperate echinoids during the peak of the spawning season.

Lifespan data for Strongylocentrotus purpuratus derive primarily from mark-recapture studies and laboratory cohorts held under controlled thermal conditions. At a rearing temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], individuals have been documented to survive for up to 25,550 days [am = up to 25,550 days], which is equivalent to approximately 70 years. This exceptional longevity places the purple sea urchin among the most long-lived of all echinoderms, a trait that is likely linked to its low metabolic rate, the structural integrity of its calcareous test, and a generalist herbivorous diet that buffers against seasonal food shortages. The maximum lifespan in the wild is probably somewhat shorter than the laboratory maximum due to predation pressure from sea otters, starfish, and large crabs, as well as the risk of storm-driven dislodgement. Nonetheless, the capacity for extreme longevity means that a single cohort can contribute to the reproductive output of a local kelp bed population for many decades.

The wet weight of a newly metamorphosed juvenile of Strongylocentrotus purpuratus, essentially the mass at the transition from pelagic larva to benthic recruit, is approximately 0.000000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000000268 grams]. This minute body mass, equivalent to just 268 nanograms, underscores the enormous size disparity between the founder individual and the asymptotic adult. The initial skeletal plates of the juvenile test are barely visible under a dissecting microscope, and the newly settled sea urchin must immediately locate a suitable microhabitat within the kelp holdfast or under cobble to avoid being swept away by currents. Once settled, the juvenile begins a rapid phase of allometric growth, increasing its test diameter by several millimetres within the first year post-metamorphosis. Reaching the pubertal test diameter of 2.5 centimetres [Lp = 2.5 centimetres] and the corresponding pubertal wet weight of 7.3 grams [Wwp = 7.3 grams] may take several years under natural food conditions, with growth rates strongly modulated by local temperature and algal availability. The maximum recorded adult mass of 465 grams [Wwi = 465 grams] and the final test diameter of 10 centimetres [Li = 10 centimetres] are among the largest documented for any echinoid in the northeastern Pacific, reflecting the extraordinary capacity for continuous somatic growth over a multi-decadal lifespan.
